pages.text:
Tanay Gada 
B.Tech CS 2026 
 
 
INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE 
 
 
 
Location: Bangalore, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Pune (required to fill preference form) 
Duration: 2 months(8 weeks) 
Stipend: 75k per month 
One time relocation compensation at start of internship: 50k

On-campus Hiring: 
Every year, JPMC recruits interns and full-time employees on campus 
through a 24 hr hackathon Code for Good. During the hackathon, Teams 
work together to develop technological solutions for challenges faced by 
non-profit organizations. 
 
Eligibility Criteria: 
1.​ Streams or Specializations: Computer Science & Information 
Technology 
2.​ CGPA: Minimum aggregate 8.5 CGPA [up to the registration 
deadline, for us it was upto sem 2] Officially they said 8.5 
cgpa, but it was mostly 8.7+ 
 
Timeline: 
➢​ Registration Process: 18 March to 20 March 
➢​ Online Coding Test: This time they’ve sent links to students in batches. Mine 
was in the 1st batch. (5 April to 8 April window)  
➢​ Video Interview: 18 April to 22nd April window 
➢​ Code for Good Shortlist announcement: 29th May 
➢​ Code for Good Event: 15 June to 16 June (saturday-sunday) 
➢​ Internship Shortlist announcement: 27th August

Online Coding Test(60 minutes): 
 
It was not a proctored test. Audio - Video was not captured  
The 2 questions I were asked during the coding round are as follows:

Question 1(Easy Difficulty) 
 
Server Selection: 
Some developers want to deploy their application on different servers with a load 
balancer in the front. There are n servers to choose from where the number of 
requests that can be handled by the ith server is server[i]. The number of 
requests served by any server is a power of 2 i.e., 1, 2, 4, 8,... 
Given an array server and an integer expected_load, find the minimum number 
of servers that must be chosen such that the total sum of requests served by all 
the chosen servers is exactly equal to the expected_load. If there is no 
combination of servers that can serve exactly expected_load requests, report -1 
as the answer 
Example: 
n = 4, servers = [1, 1, 2, 4], expected_load = 3 
output: 2 
it is optimal to choose server[0] and server[2] or server[1] and server[2] 
 
My Approach: 
I took around 7-8 mins to correctly submit it and passed all the test cases. On 
carefully reading the long question for 2 times, i understood it was a very easy 
greedy question 
So I first sort the server array in ascending order and then start iterating from the 
end of the server array. Used these conditions 
if(expected_cost>= server[i]) 
​
expected_cost-=server[i] 
​
countOfServers++ 
if(expected_cost==0) 
​
return countOfServers

Question 2 (Easy Difficulty) 
Given an array, reduce the array to a single element 
In each operation, pick two indices i and j (where i != j ) and 
​
append the value of a[i] + a[j] to the array 
​
delete a[i] and a[j] from the array 
The cost of each operation is a[i] + a[j]. Find the minimum possible cost to 
reduce the array 
example 
array: [25, 10, 20] 
pick 10 and 20, cost = 30, array = [25,30] 
pick 25 and 30, cost = 55 array = [55] 
totalCost = 30 + 55 = 85 
My Approach 
Solved this in 7-8 mins and passed all test cases. Used priority queue to choose & 
delete 2 smallest elements and inserted their sum to the priority queue.  
 
My Observation: 
There were a set of 8 - 10 questions from which randomly 2 questions were asked 
to each student. So you can consider checking questions asked to your friends 
and then attempt OA. Every question could be solved by brute force and was very 
easy. Submissions with partial test cases may also help clear OA. There was one 
question asked to my friend - it involved string manipulation and was very time 
consuming to do in c++. Python helped there.

Video Interview (10 minutes): 
The next step of the recruiting process is a video interview, powered by HireVue. 
In this HireVue interview, you will be asked to record video responses to 2 
interview questions. 
The types of questions in video interviews are pretty standard and repeated for 
most of the candidates, some of them are: 
1.​ What is your biggest achievement till now and what learning did you get 
from the same? 
2.​ Talk about a recent experience where your friend needs the help to 
understand the concept that you’ve understood. Describe how you taught 
him? 
3.​ When did you change your communication approach with a teammate or 
colleague? What was the outcome ? 
4.​ When was your last successful presentation or speech? What was the 
subject? What made it successful? 
I used my hackathon experiences and the COC DSA workshop (where I taught a 
topic) to answer the HireVue questions. I did fumble a bit, but I feel that my clarity 
of thought, honesty, and real-life experiences helped me clear HireVue. I 
expressed my experiences well by using hand gestures and expressive facial 
expressions. There was no requirement for specific attire; I wore a white shirt 
during the interview. Make sure to sit in a well-lit area and adjust the webcam so 
that your upper body, up to the chest, is visible. 
A question appears on the screen, and we are given a few seconds (I think it was 
around 30 seconds, but I’m not sure) to prepare. After that, the video recording 
starts automatically. Once the first recording is done, we can watch it and have 
the option to re-record. If we choose to record a second time, the first recording is 
deleted, and the second recording is automatically submitted. We do not get to 
see the second recording.

Shortlist Results for CFG: 
The final list of all shortlisted students came out about a month later(29 
May) from the video interview submission, 13 students were selected for 
the hackathon. 
 
Code for Good 2023 Hackathon (15th and 16th June) 
We had an offline hackathon, and we were the first batch to be allowed into the 
workspace of the new Goregaon office for the Code For Good Hackathon. 
Pre-Hackathon Arrangements: 
One week before the actual hackathon, we received a link to join the Slack 
channel. Four days before the event, we were given the team mappings. 
My team consisted of 3 boys and 4 girls. We had a Google Meet a couple of days 
before the hackathon to discuss each member’s proficiency. Here’s how our 
team looked: 
-​ 1 boy: Only C++ (Competitive Programming specialist on Codeforces), no 
development experience. 
-​ 1 girl: HTML/CSS, JavaScript, GSAP (had participated in a couple of 
hackathons). 
-​ 1 girl: Skilled in PowerPoint and Figma design. 
-​ 2 girls: HTML/CSS, JavaScript. 
-​ 1 boy: Was then watching backend tutorials (MongoDB and Node) 
-​ Me: Only Frontend (React), Authentication, and Integration experience (had 
participated in 3 hackathons). 
We mutually discussed and decided on the roles and responsibilities. The 4 girls 
were assigned to frontend development, and the 3 boys took up backend 
development. 
Although I had no prior experience in backend development, I voluntarily took up 
the responsibility because no one else in the team was willing to lead the 
backend.

During hackathon: 
We were asked to reach JPMC’s Goregaon office on 15th June before 12:30 PM. I 
recommend arriving at least an hour early so you can enjoy the brunch, collect 
your preferred size of the JPMC CFG T-shirt, and bond with your team. I met my 
teammates upon arrival but had to skip brunch because I was a bit late. 
Each team was seated together, and one or two mentors (JPMC employees) 
were assigned to each team and sat with us. The mentors were extremely helpful 
— they monitored our progress, assisted with both technical and managerial 
challenges, shared insights about JPMC, and were incredibly friendly and 
approachable. 
The event began with an introduction from the JPMC Code For Good team, where 
they spoke about JPMC’s values, goals, various initiatives, and organizational 
culture. While it might seem a bit long, it’s worth paying attention to — it gives a 
great sense of what it’s like to work at JPMC and helps you understand the 
company better as a potential employer. 
There were three NGOs participating in CFG 2024 Mumbai. Coordinators from 
each organization provided insights into their work and shared detailed 
information about the challenges they were facing — areas that lacked proper 
technical solutions. These formed the basis of our problem statements. 
We were given 15 minutes to discuss within our team and submit a Google Form 
ranking our preferred problem statements (allotted on a first-come-first-serve 
basis). After the allocation, teams were grouped based on their chosen problem 
statements and were given 30 to 45 minutes to interact with the NGO 
coordinators to clarify all doubts. 
Our team was assigned to the EAGL Livelihood Foundation, an NGO that works 
with tribal communities. Their challenge was to digitize data-related operations 
and develop a system for efficient tracking and management. 
Try to note down all the requirements in your diary during this phase. A solution 
that effectively addresses the core problems and requirements is far more 
valuable than one with unique features that don’t contribute to solving the actual 
issue.

The Coding Phase Begins!! 
On Day 1, we were assigned a mentor who began by asking each of us to 
introduce ourselves and share our hobbies and interests. The environment was 
very welcoming. 
We were provided with large chart papers/sheets to brainstorm our solution and 
were also given access to cabins and focus rooms within the JPMC office — a 
great help for focused collaboration. 
We had an intense 3-hour discussion at the beginning, during which we covered 
several important aspects: 
1.​ Understanding the requirements of the organization 
2.​ Defining the scope of the project — this was especially crucial since our 
assigned NGO, EAGL Livelihood Foundation, had coordinators who weren’t 
very structured and listed around 10–12 different problems their 
organization was facing 
3.​ Sketching wireframes for the solution 
4.​ Identifying team members’ strengths and accordingly distributing the 
work 
Make sure to actively express your thoughts and ideas during team discussions — 
including in front of your mentor. This plays a significant role in your overall 
evaluation and can influence your selection. 
At the same time, be selfless. Never try to defame or disrespect any teammate, 
and avoid seeking attention from mentors in a negative or forced way. Maintain a 
positive and collaborative attitude, and be willing to step out of your comfort 
zone to support your teammates. Genuine teamwork and mutual respect go a 
long way in building not just a great solution, but also a strong impression. 
At the beginning, I advised the frontend team to ensure that the UI looked like it 
was built by a single developer. I suggested that everyone use the same UI library 
so that the components remained consistent and the overall design felt unified. I 
also recommended keeping the interface minimalistic, considering that the 
platform would be used in low-network areas. 
I reiterated these points twice during the development phase, but they weren’t 
followed. Instead of repeating myself further, I chose not to bring it up again.

It’s important to offer guidance and suggestions to your team, but avoid nagging 
or complaining about teammates to the mentor. Doing so builds mutual respect 
within the team. When you maintain a positive and respectful attitude, your 
teammates are more likely to support each other and work collaboratively. 
I took on multiple key responsibilities during the hackathon, including: 
1.​ Implementing role-based authentication (for which I already had a 
template prepared from previous hackathons) 
2.​ Designing the database schema (in collaboration with another teammate) 
3.​ Building APIs (again, alongside a teammate) 
4.​ Integrating the frontend with the backend 
I ended up handling more tasks compared to some of my teammates. This was 
primarily because many of them lacked the confidence to take ownership — they 
were concerned that failing in a task might hurt their chances of selection for the 
internship. 
At the time, my mindset was a bit different. I believed that better companies 
would come to VJTI for internships, so I wasn’t very serious about this opportunity. 
Honestly, my goal back then was just to win the iPad 🥲. But I now realize that this 
mentality was wrong. We should respect every opportunity that comes our way 
and give it our best — especially the first one we get. 
None of my teammates were familiar with Git and GitHub, and I was also a bit 
underconfident when it came to resolving merge conflicts. Throughout the 
hackathon, I helped my teammates push and merge their code—sometimes 
even seeking assistance from a mentor to resolve tricky conflicts. 
During our initial frontend team meeting, three out of four members said they had 
some knowledge of React.js and planned to brush up on it in the two days before 
the hackathon. However, during the event, I realized that none of them were 
familiar with essential concepts like React Router or Hooks 🙂. So, I took the 
initiative to show them how these work, shared a helpful YouTube tutorial, and 
supported them in troubleshooting their errors and doubts. 
We had two mentors during the hackathon—one for Day 1 and another for Day 2. 
Each teammate had a one-on-one interview with both mentors. The first mentor 
took every team member individually into her cabin/focus room for a discussion. I 
was the last person to be interviewed.

My First One-On-One Interview 
I was asked about my interests, sports, and my future plans. I also shared my 
expectations for myself until the end of my B.Tech at VJTI. 
The mentor openly mentioned that she felt our team was not very strong and 
asked me how I was feeling about it. Initially, I agreed and went along with the 
flow of the conversation 🤡. But then, I cleverly shifted the perspective by pointing 
out that each team member has strengths—they just weren’t placed in the right 
roles. I explained that if the teams had been formed based on proficiency and 
experience with the relevant tech stack, everyone would have had a better 
chance to contribute effectively. Nonetheless, I emphasized that everyone still 
has a lot to learn and grow. 
She then asked me to explain what Competitive Programming is, as I had 
mentioned my interest in it earlier. Later, she inquired why I have experience 
mainly working on frontend and integration, but not the backend. 
At the end, she said, “Good, keep it up. I’ve received positive feedback from your 
teammates about you. Coordinate tasks well and try to complete the project.” 
That left me feeling good and very excited. 
My helpful nature and positive attitude helped me create a good impression 
and earn the respect of my teammates, which led them to praise me during 
their one-on-one interviews. 
I ended up solving everyone’s doubts and errors, pushing code, handling merge 
conflicts, designing the database schema, and integrating the role-based 
authentication with the landing page on Day 1 (before dinner). During dinner, we 
discussed and planned our workflow. Since I had limited time and felt that the 
integration tasks should be shared, I asked two frontend team members to learn 
promises and how to use fetch/axios. 
Starting at midnight, the teammate who knew backend and I referred to YouTube 
tutorials and used ChatGPT to quickly develop and test the APIs. We completed 
the backend work by 3 a.m. After a 30-minute break, we helped the frontend 
team by demonstrating how fetch/axios works, explaining React hooks like 
useState, useEffect, and useContext, and gave them hands-on experience. 
The mentor we had for Day 2 was the Vice President, with around 15 years of

experience at JPMC and 25 years overall. I had a one-on-one interview with him 
in the morning. 
My Second One-On-One Interview 
The mentor mainly discussed my future plans, asking if I intended to pursue 
further studies (postgraduate). I shared that I wish to do an MBA or possibly an 
MS if I develop a strong interest in machine learning during my third year after 
securing an internship offer. He jokingly asked, “Then why should we hire you if 
you’re just going to leave?” 🤡I explained that pursuing postgraduate studies 
typically requires at least a couple of years of work experience, and I believe 
JPMC is the best fit for me during that time. I also mentioned that if I can learn 
and develop my skills by working at JPMC—which would give me practical 
experience beyond what I’d gain from business school—I might cancel my plans 
for an MBA. He also asked about how I got into VJTI and my journey with HSC, CET, 
and JEE ranks. 
The employees at JPMC Mumbai consider VJTI to be a very, very good college. So, 
the chances of selection for a VJTian are already around 50% even before the 
start of CodeForGood. 
My teammate handling backend and I managed to fully integrate two pages by 6 
am. I was completely drained and frustrated seeing the frontend team 
struggle—although they knew React, they didn’t grasp key concepts like useState, 
useEffect, and useContext hooks 😭😭😭. I finally took a long, well-needed 1-hour 
break (my first break during CFG), caught up with some VJTI batchmates, and 
realized many teams faced similar challenges. 
After the break, I integrated another page by 7 am, but the mentor then advised 
us to shift focus to preparing the presentation and to leave the last page and 
frontend consistency for later. 
Our evaluation was scheduled around 10 am. We started building the 
presentation from 7:30 am. I suggested and created a couple of flowcharts to 
clearly explain our solution—one illustrating the user’s perspective and another 
outlining the technical architecture. I also recommended including the database 
schema model in the slides. We decided that only two team members would 
present, and those two prepared thoroughly for it. 
Unfortunately, we didn’t win the hackathon. Even the Day 2 mentor accepted this

and tried to leave before our presentation but was asked to stay 😂😂😂. 
During the presentation and evaluation, we showcased our working prototype 
and MongoDB Atlas collections. We were also asked about why we chose the 
specific tech stack for our project. 
The hackathon included multiple sessions that were intended to be fun, but 
honestly, they weren’t that enjoyable 🙂. However, the snacks (chocolates, hot 
chocolate, Dark Fantasy, coffee, biscuits…) and meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner) 
were available round the clock, which helped keep us going.

My tips for the hackathon: 
1.​ Always speak out your opinions — Even if you think your ideas are obvious 
or might not be the best fit, voicing them is essential for effective 
brainstorming and innovation. 
2.​ Support and prioritize your team — Teamwork is crucial. Every major 
software product is built through collaboration, so putting your team’s 
success above individual ego leads to better results. 
3.​ Avoid trying to impress mentors by quantifying your work or putting 
down others — The best way to gain respect is by being genuine, staying 
humble, helping others, and earning praise through your actions. 
4.​ Take ownership of difficult tasks — If there’s a challenging task that 
nobody wants, step up and do it. Even if you fail, it shows courage and 
commitment. This earned me praise from my mentor, and integration work 
is especially valued since it’s complex and risky. 
5.​ Software engineering goes beyond coding — It involves understanding the 
real problems, designing relevant solutions, managing the team, and 
ensuring smooth collaboration. 
6.​ Keep communication flowing — Regularly suggest ideas, discuss progress, 
replan if needed, and motivate your teammates to keep everyone aligned 
and productive. 
7.​ Prepare by reading past interview experiences and hackathon insights — 
I missed this before the event and wasn’t fully prepared for the one-on-one 
mentor interviews. Preparation helps in answering questions thoughtfully 
and confidently. 
8.​ If i would have to go into CFG again, i would get exposure to these things 
a.​ Frontend (routing, API management, component state flow) 
b.​ Backend (schema planning, API development, role based auth) 
c.​ Git/GitHub (especially resolving conflicts) 
d.​ Gemini API Usage 
9.​ This experience was based on team in which all members were newbie 
development skillwise(including myself). Consider reading multiple 
experiences as they change based on the team which one gets.

Internship Offer 
Out of our 7-member team, 3 of us secured internships — including myself. 
Looking back, it’s clear that technical skills alone don’t guarantee success. What 
truly made the difference was: 
1.​ Effective communication 
2.​ Strong teamwork 
3.​ A helping mindset 
4.​ The willingness to grow and adapt under pressure 
Yes, coding can be learned through tutorials and personal projects. But a growth 
mindset and collaborative nature — those are qualities that can’t be taught 
overnight. They’re what mentors, companies, and teams value the most in the 
long run. 
The real key to doing well isn’t being the smartest or the fastest — it’s about lifting 
your team, taking initiative, staying grounded, and learning from every 
interaction.

A better way to answer questions about future study plans is: 
“As of now, I haven’t made a concrete decision about pursuing a postgraduate 
degree. My primary focus is to gain real-world experience and contribute 
meaningfully to the organization I join. If, at some point in my career, I feel that a 
Master’s or MBA would significantly help me grow or provide a fresh perspective, I 
will definitely consider it. But for now, I’m more focused on learning, growing, and 
making an impact through work.” 
Directly telling them that you plan to pursue a postgraduate degree can lower 
your chances of selection. 
 
JPMC selection through CFG isn’t just about coding skills — it also evaluates your 
character. I believe these qualities should be reflected through your presence at 
CFG: 
1.​ Be a team player 
2.​ Stay calm, composed, and positive under pressure 
3.​ Motivate your team, even when things aren’t going well 
4.​ Help others learn and grow 
5.​ Be selfless and collaborative 
6.​ Be optimistic — view every setback as a learning opportunity​
 
I stayed true to myself, supported my team, and expressed who I really am — and 
I got selected. It’s really that simple. 
VJTI holds strong brand value among companies with offices in Maharashtra — 
including JPMC, Morgan Stanley, Citi, BNY, NPCI, and others. 
VJTI students truly carry an aura among the employees of these companies 
Interviewers genuinely respect and value VJTI students. They often speak highly 
of the institute and are more inclined to select VJTIans. So, stay calm, be 
confident, and express yourself freely as we grow when we make mistakes and 
step out of our comfort

Final advice 
The internship drive phase can be truly exhausting and emotionally draining, 
especially when faced with a series of rejections. Preparing well in advance is key. 
I personally got a reality check after each rejection — but with every rejection, I 
learned, grew, and became better. So, take each rejection as an opportunity to 
improve. 
Form a focused group of 3–5 friends and practice together regularly. Conduct 
mock interviews and, most importantly, celebrate and appreciate each other’s 
successes. I’m proud to say that all four members of my group secured 
internships at good companies. 
This is the time when you lay the foundation for your interview preparation. During 
the placement season, time will be limited due to ongoing summer internships, so 
the effort you put into internship prep now will greatly benefit you later.  
 
Analyzing setbacks, identifying areas of improvement, and 
consistently putting in effort — that’s what truly leads to 
growth and success.
